title: Having trouble with multiplayer.
author: Brief-Kangaroo4960
selftext: I'm using ChatGPT Astra and I had it make a simple pixel art game with multiplayer. I tried multiple times in different ways, but the game always has multiple different problems, like the players see their skills being cast from where they were a second ago, or the non-hosts always seeing things a few steps behind, or consistent effects look like they are blinking for the non-host. Has anyone been able to successfully make a multiplayer game that runs smoothly using AI?

comments.author: joeld42
comments.body:
Multiplayer is very hard, AI does a great job if you know what to ask for. I'm working on a multiplayer game with pretty hard requirements and it's working great, but it's the kind of thing I've done before as a dev (it would take me a year without AI though). To be honest, I would suggest you start with a template or existing middleware, that will give the AI some examples and suggest the pattern to follow. What kind of game is it? I can suggest some things to ask it.  Depends on your genre but you might want to start by telling it "make the game server authoritative, and only display verified state" (which is not always what you want, it's not the case for my game, but it's usually a good start).

For things like spell effects, have a delay before the casting, so that if the cast starts, at time X, you start the animation for the local player immediately, but the cast doesn't actually happen until a few frames later, when it has time to propogate to all the peers.  If the game can deal with a few frames of delay that is usually a good way to handle it, if it's very timing specific you need something like rollback.

The fundamental problem with multiplayer is that no matter how fast your network is, you're always dealing with information that is a fraction of a second behind. You need a strategy to handle this.

replies.author: Brief-Kangaroo4960
replies.body: It's a 2D pixel-art isometric game where everything is modular. You get to draw pixel art and then open the skill menu and pick projectile and damage on hit with the image you drew, and it becomes a spell then use it. You can make NPCs and objects tiles etc. Basically, building your own little game or map with your friends. The whole idea was to have a place where you can draw pixel art, share it with friends, and try it out to motivate everyone to draw better and better things to show off. It's using Steam P2P networking with a host-authoritative client-server, built in Godot 4.3.

replies.author: joeld42
replies.body:
I forgot the best tip -- use a network conditioner like "clumsy" to simulate delay, or ask your agent to build that in for testing. It's a lot easier to notice (both for you and the agent) when thing aren't working with realistic delay, just testing with localhost a lot of things work that wouldn't otherwise. 

For your game, it sounds like it's host authoritative already so that's good. It depends on each effect, but for for a projectile you might be able to calculate ahead where the sim "hits" in the future, and then send that, so the local player will see it immediately and a remote player might not see the first few frames but will see the same result. Basically if you can build in a little time window between the player's input and the effect on the simulation, that will give the peers a chance to catch up.

You can also run a local copy of the simulation for the local player, and only change when the server differs, so when a player that is not the host does a spell or something, it will react immediately. The important thing is that you never get in a situations where things desync.
